questions.sentence: I noticed that he spoke English with an Australian accent.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
options: Nominal clause — postmodifier of an adjective
questions.explanation: The that-clause answers “What did I notice?” and completes the verb “noticed”. It behaves like a noun phrase in Direct Object function.

questions.sentence: What you want is impossible.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
options: Nominal clause — postmodifier of an adjective
questions.explanation: The that-clause states the content of the noun “fact”; it does not identify which fact among several. This content relationship makes it appositive.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?

questions.sentence: Wherever he went, he was welcome.

questions.sentence: He spends his money as if he were rich.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?

questions.sentence: Entering the room, he noticed that the windows were open.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The subject of “Entering” is understood as “he”, and the detached non-finite clause adds a circumstance to the main clause. It is supplementive and functions as Adverbial.

questions.sentence: On arriving at the cottage, Tom found it burnt down.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The preposition plus -ing clause sets the time at which Tom found the cottage burnt down. As a whole it functions as an Adverbial.

questions.sentence: She rang up her mother to ask her to dinner.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The to-infinitival clause explains why she rang her mother, adding purpose to the main clause. It therefore functions as an Adverbial.

questions.sentence: Although always helpful, he was not much liked.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The reduced although-clause omits an overt subject and verb but preserves a concessive contrast. As a whole it functions as an Adverbial.

questions.sentence: Even if still working, the engine is not reliable.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The reduced even-if clause supplies a condition despite which the engine remains unreliable. As a whole it functions as an Adverbial.

questions.sentence: Students who work hard pass their exams.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause identifies which students are meant: those who work hard. Because it narrows the reference of “Students”, it is restrictive and functions as Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: The record I am listening to is a present from Moscow.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause identifies which record is meant, with a zero relative element understood as the object of “to”. It is a restrictive Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: Our granny of whom we were very fond died unexpectedly.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: “Whom” refers back to “Our granny”, and the clause adds information about that noun phrase. It therefore functions as a relative-clause Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: I could see no reason why I should refuse a drink.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The relative adverb “why” links the clause to “reason”, specifying the reason under discussion. The clause functions as Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: We could find no place where we could talk in peace.

targets.text: where we could talk in peace

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?

questions.sentence: I liked the present which Mrs. Thompson sent me.

questions.sentence: He is no longer the man he was.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause completes the comparison with the earlier state of “the man”; a zero relative element is understood. It functions as a relative-clause Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: Any person who wishes to see me must take an appointment.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The who-clause selects the subset of people who wish to see the speaker. Because it restricts “Any person”, it functions as a restrictive Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: The giant panda, which is to be found in the remote parts of China, lives exclusively on bamboo shoots.

targets.text: which is to be found in the remote parts of China

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The comma-set which-clause adds extra information about the already identified giant panda rather than selecting one panda. It is non-restrictive and functions as Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: The following day which was Friday he left for Belgrade.
questions.prompt: Which description best fits the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: “The following day” already identifies the day, while the which-clause adds its calendar identity. On that interpretation the clause is non-restrictive, even though commas are absent.

questions.sentence: She said that she had lost her purse.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “That” introduces the content clause after “said” but has no participant role inside it. It is therefore a complementizer.

questions.sentence: Time will show whether we are right or wrong.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “Whether” introduces an indirect yes-or-no alternative: right or wrong. That interrogative role makes it an interrogative subordinator.

questions.sentence: The question is if he feels up to the task.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: Here “if” introduces an indirect yes-or-no question after “The question is”, rather than a condition. It is an interrogative subordinator.

questions.sentence: If it weren't so cold, it would be nice.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “If” links a conditional dependent clause to the main clause. In this use it is a subordinating conjunction.

questions.sentence: As it was raining, we stayed indoors all day.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: Here “As” introduces the reason for staying indoors and connects that dependent clause to the main clause. It is a subordinating conjunction.

questions.sentence: While he has invested a lot of money in paintings, he doesn't understand very much about art.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “While” introduces a concessive dependent clause contrasting investment with understanding. It is a subordinating conjunction.

questions.sentence: Students who work hard pass their exams.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “Who” introduces the relative clause and also serves as its Subject, referring back to “Students”. That participant role makes it a relative pronoun.

questions.sentence: We could find no place where we could talk in peace.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “Where” links the relative clause to “place” and expresses location inside the clause. It is a relative adverb.

questions.sentence: The best thing would be to tell everybody.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: “To” directly introduces the base-form verb “tell”, marking a to-infinitival clause. It is not a preposition in this use.

questions.sentence: He said ∅ he had lost his mind.
questions.prompt: What type of clause marker is highlighted?
questions.explanation: The content clause has no pronounced marker before “he”, but an omitted “that” could be supplied. The marker is therefore represented as zero.

questions.sentence: He promised that every question would be answered.

targets.text: that every question would be answered

questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause contains the finite verb group “would be answered” and is introduced by “that”. These features make it a finite that-clause.

questions.sentence: I think you have some influence on her.

targets.text: you have some influence on her

questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause has the finite verb “have” but no pronounced “that”; inserting “that” after “think” is possible. It is a finite zero-that clause.

questions.sentence: How the accident happened is a mystery.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause is introduced by the wh-word “How” and contains the finite verb “happened”. It is therefore a finite wh-clause.

questions.sentence: I am not sure whether that will come out all right.

targets.text: whether that will come out all right

questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: “Whether” introduces an indirect alternative and “will come” is finite. The structure is a finite whether/if-clause.

questions.sentence: The best thing would be to tell everybody.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The marker “to” is followed by the base-form verb “tell”, so the highlighted unit is a to-infinitival clause.

questions.sentence: I heard her sing.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: After “heard her”, the verb “sing” appears in its base form without “to”. That makes the highlighted unit a bare infinitival clause.

questions.sentence: Knowing my temper, I didn't reply.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The clause is headed by the -ing form “Knowing” and has the understood Subject “I”. Its structure is an -ing clause.

questions.sentence: He left without saying goodbye.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: “Without” is a preposition followed by the -ing clause “saying goodbye”. The whole highlighted unit has a preposition + -ing-clause structure.

questions.sentence: Too nervous to reply, he stared at the floor.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The highlighted unit has no finite verb: the adjective phrase “Too nervous” is expanded by a to-infinitive. It is a reduced / verbless clause.

questions.sentence: She was as friendly as she had ever been.
questions.prompt: What is the structure of the highlighted clause?
questions.explanation: The pattern “as … as” sets up a comparison, and the highlighted clause supplies the comparison point. Its structure is comparative.

questions.sentence: That he is rich doesn't mean anything to them.
questions.prompt: What function does the highlighted clause have in the larger sentence?
questions.explanation: The that-clause is what “doesn’t mean anything”; it occupies the position normally filled by a noun phrase Subject. Its function is Subject.

questions.sentence: He promised that every question would be answered.

targets.text: that every question would be answered

questions.prompt: What function does the highlighted clause have in the larger sentence?
questions.explanation: The that-clause answers “What did he promise?” and completes the verb “promised”. Its function in the larger clause is Direct Object.

questions.sentence: This is what he said.
questions.prompt: What function does the highlighted clause have in the larger sentence?
questions.explanation: After the linking verb “is”, the nominal relative clause identifies what “This” is. It therefore functions as Subject Complement.

questions.sentence: She sang as she drove home.
questions.prompt: What function does the highlighted clause have in the larger sentence?
questions.explanation: The as-clause tells when or under what accompanying circumstance she sang. It modifies the main event and functions as Adverbial.

questions.sentence: The man I spoke to is an accountant in our firm.
questions.prompt: What function does the highlighted clause have in the larger sentence?
questions.explanation: The clause identifies which man is meant and follows the noun phrase it modifies. Its function is Postmodifier.

questions.sentence: I heard her sing.
questions.prompt: What function does the highlighted clause have in the larger sentence?
questions.explanation: The bare infinitival clause “sing” completes the perception construction “heard her …”. In this analysis it has the combined label OC / Clausal object.

questions.sentence: George smashed a window in his father's car.
questions.prompt: Can the highlighted phrase be assigned one clear sentence-element function from this sentence alone?
questions.explanation: The prepositional phrase can be linked to more than one part of the sentence. More context is needed before assigning one function with confidence.

questions.sentence: The fight for the world championship title is tomorrow at 11 p.m.
questions.prompt: What is the function of the highlighted word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The time expression completes the subject description after “is”, so it is treated here as a Subject Complement.
